```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Adapted closely from Ali Johnston's MT5751 L21 SCR I demo.
# Preparation and simulation are in code/prepare_intro_practical.R;
# Students use secr and sf::st_read for the survey boundary, plus prepared TRI inputs.
# Nelder-Mead accommodates the original raster scale of TRI without trial-step overflow.
library(secr)
library(knitr)
preview_captures <- read.csv("data/practical/snow_leopard_captures.csv")
knitr::opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = "figures/02-scr-", dev = "pdf",
                      echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      size="scriptsize")
def.chunk.hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("chunk")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(chunk = function(x, options) {
  x <- def.chunk.hook(x, options)
  if (options$size != "normalsize")
    paste0("\n\\begingroup\n\\", options$size, "\n\n", x, "\n\\endgroup\n") else x
})
hook_output <- knit_hooks$get("output")
knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  lines <- options$output.lines
  if (is.null(lines)) return(hook_output(x, options))
  x <- strsplit(x, "\n")[[1]]
  if (length(lines) == 1) {
    if (length(x) > lines) x <- c(head(x, lines), "...")
  } else {
    x <- c("...", x[intersect(lines, seq_along(x))], "...")
  }
  hook_output(paste(c(x, ""), collapse = "\n"), options)
})
```

# Collecting data for SCR

## Overview

1. Define the survey region and analysis goals.
2. Decide on detector locations and effort.
    a. Macro-level: which landscapes to survey?
    b. Micro-level: where to place detectors within them?
3. Agree and follow a data collection protocol.
    a. Mainly camera traps; briefly, genetic sampling.
4. Manage the data for analysis.
    a. Individual identification, records and GIS layers.

**Aim:** a starting framework for SCR surveys in Kyrgyzstan.
A full survey also needs local planning, a pilot and specialist advice.

<!-- Main source throughout this field section:
Sharma, K., Borchers, D., Mackenzie, D., Durbach, I., Sutherland, C., Nichols, J.,
Lovari, S., Zhi, L., Ale, S., Khan, A. A., Modaqiq, W., McCarthy, T.,
Alexander, J. S. & Mishra, C. (2020). PAWS Guidelines. GSLEP.
Further reading: further_reading/PAWS-guidelines-2020.pdf.
Page references below are PRINTED pages, not PDF viewer page numbers.
The overview combines region and goals into one planning step, retaining the
four-step field workflow. General principles are adapted from the snow-leopard
guidelines; species-specific figures are examples, not universal prescriptions.
Kyrgyzstan examples and exercises below are teaching
adaptations, not a prescribed national monitoring protocol. -->

## 1. Start with a question you can answer

\roomyitems

- **Example:** how many animals of our target species have activity centres
  in this mapped landscape during this survey season?
- Agree which animals count (e.g. adults or independent animals), and choose
  a method that can identify individuals reliably.
- Is the priority abundance, habitat differences, or change over time?
  Each needs a suitable design and enough data.
- For trends, plan repeat surveys in comparable seasons, with consistent
  boundaries and protocols.

\alert{The number of different individuals detected is a minimum count,
not an estimate of all animals present.}

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 9--13 (region, goals, resources) and
pp. 44--47 (SCR inference). The independent-animal target is an example to
agree before sampling, not a claim that dependent young can never be modelled.
Abundance here refers to activity centres inside a defined reporting region;
animals photographed near its edge may have centres outside it. -->

## 1. Draw the boundary; check what is feasible

\roomyitems

- Map the region of interest, habitat, valleys, ridges, settlements and access.
  A reserve boundary need not be a biological boundary.
- Include less promising habitat; surveying only known strongholds limits
  where results can be applied.
- Plan with rangers and local communities: permissions, access, livestock
  movements, camera security and safe routes.
- Budget for deployment, checks, retrieval, image identification and analysis;
  for genetics, include laboratory costs and likely failed samples.

**Decide before fieldwork:** who coordinates the survey, manages the data
and helps with the analysis?

<!-- Source: PAWS (2020), pp. 9--13, 20--23, 25--30.
Community coordination, mountain access and team responsibilities are practical
teaching adaptations for Kyrgyzstan. Distinguish access restrictions from
unsuitable habitat: an inaccessible valley is not an empty valley.
Obtain any required reserve/border access and sample permissions locally. -->

## 2. Macro-level design: choose landscapes fairly

\roomyitems

- For a single landscape, plan coverage of that landscape.
- For a much larger region, select several survey areas using a
  **representative sampling design**, with statistical help.
- Map candidate areas first; include different habitats, human pressures
  and expected animal densities.
- Use random or spatially balanced selection, possibly within strata;
  agree how inaccessible selections will be handled.

\alert{A few well-studied reserves cannot automatically represent
all of Kyrgyzstan.}

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 14--19, 23--24;
GSLEP, Macro Level Design Tools:
https://globalsnowleopard.org/gslep-projects/paws/paws-resources/macro-level-design-tools/
PAWS discusses macro-design mainly for regions >10,000 km2; this is a scale
guide, not a threshold that makes convenience sampling valid below it.
Retain inclusion probabilities and departures from the selected sample.
National extrapolation and combining arrays require support beyond this class. -->

## 2. Micro-level design: seek spatial recaptures

\roomyitems[0.3em]

- Spread stations across the selected landscape and its habitat types.
- Keep neighbouring stations close enough that the **same individual can be
  detected at several stations**: a spatial recapture.
- Start with spacing around **1--2$\sigma$**, where $\sigma$ describes the
  species' movement scale. Use local studies or pilot data to guide this.
- Low detection may favour closer spacing: for elusive snow leopards,
  PAWS suggests **3--5 km**. Test this locally, including for smaller-ranging animals.
- Balance spatial recaptures against landscape coverage; avoid both a tiny
  dense array and widely isolated stations.
- Simulation can be an important tool here.


<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 20--23;
Durbach, I., Micro-level survey design for secr, GSLEP/SLT cheatsheet:
https://globalsnowleopard.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/How-to-choose-where-to-setup-camera-traps-survey-design_-.pdf
The cheatsheet suggests 1--2 sigma. For a half-normal detection function,
sigma is the spatial scale of declining detection, related to space use;
it is not a daily travel distance or a home-range radius. It also depends on
the detection-function parameterisation and survey period.
Efford, M. G. & Boulanger, J. (2019). Fast evaluation of study designs for
spatially explicit capture--recapture. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10:
1529--1545. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13239
Closer spacing may be useful when baseline detection is low; PAWS's 3--5 km
example is not necessarily below 1--2 sigma at every snow leopard site.
Durbach, I., Borchers, D., Sutherland, C. & Sharma, K. (2021).
Fast, flexible alternatives to regular grid designs for spatial capture--recapture.
Methods in Ecology and Evolution 12: 298--310.
https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13517
Nawaz, M. A., Khan, B. U., Mahmood, A., Younas, M., Din, J. U. &
Sutherland, C. (2021). An empirical demonstration of the effect of study design
on density estimations. Scientific Reports 11: 13104.
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-92361-2
Spacing is not a universal prescription. The smallest relevant movement scale
matters; a layout suited only to wide-ranging males can miss female recaptures.
Do not substitute walking-route distance for model distance without discussing
the detection model. Non-Euclidean models are beyond this introduction. -->

## 2. Same equipment; different information

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.72cm,y=0.72cm]
\foreach \xx/\label in {0/{Too concentrated},4.5/{Too dispersed},9/{Balance to test}} {
  \draw[gray] (\xx,0) rectangle +(4,3.6);
  \node[font=\small] at (\xx+2,4) {\label};
}
\foreach \xx/\yy in {1.5/1.4,2/1.4,2.5/1.4,1.5/2,2/2,2.5/2}
  \fill[teal] (\xx,\yy) circle (0.09);
\foreach \xx/\yy in {4.8/0.4,6.5/0.4,8.2/0.4,4.8/3.2,6.5/3.2,8.2/3.2}
  \fill[teal] (\xx,\yy) circle (0.09);
\foreach \xx/\yy in {9.7/0.9,10.5/0.9,10.1/1.7,11.8/2,12.6/2,12.2/2.8}
  \fill[teal] (\xx,\yy) circle (0.09);
\foreach \xx in {2,6.5,10.1,12.2}
  \draw[orange,thick] (\xx,1.7) circle (0.9);
\node[align=center,font=\footnotesize] at (2,-0.65) {Limited landscape\\coverage};
\node[align=center,font=\footnotesize] at (6.5,-0.65) {Few opportunities\\for spatial recaptures};
\node[align=center,font=\footnotesize] at (11,-0.65) {Coverage plus\\nearby neighbours};
\end{tikzpicture}

```

\small
Dots: stations. Circles: illustrative animal space use.
Schematic only; no scale or recommended cluster layout.

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 20--23, especially Fig. 6;
Durbach et al. (2021), https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13517.
Original teaching schematic, not a copied figure or an optimized design.
Six stations in each panel. Clusters can help but do not guarantee adequate
sample size, habitat representation, or estimation of movement scale. -->

## 2. Choose a season and a realistic duration

\roomyitems

- Use one reasonably short session for a closed-population analysis:
  few births, deaths or permanent changes in membership; reasonably stable
  activity centres.
- Animals can move between stations and across the survey boundary:
  **ordinary movement is expected**.
- Choose duration for the species' life history and seasonal movements;
  balance enough detections against closure and practical access.
- Deploy stations in a coordinated period. **Record detector start/end dates
  and failures** so unequal effort can be modelled.

Longer deployment may add photographs but weaken the closure assumption.

<!-- Source: PAWS (2020), pp. 5--8, 21--22, 33--34.
PAWS's example combines >500 km2, 30--40 stations and 2--3 months. These are
experience-based starting values, not independent minimum requirements or a
guarantee of estimability. Duration must be chosen for the target species,
not transferred unchanged from snow leopards. Stable activity centres are part of the introductory closed SCR
model. Multi-season/open-population models need additional planning. -->

## 2. Pilot before committing the full budget

\small

- Test access, installation time, battery life and image quality in the
  conditions expected during the main survey.
- Check how many **identifiable individuals** are recorded and how many
  appear at **more than one station**.
- Review gaps in coverage and unsuccessful sites; few detections may mean
  low density, poor placement, equipment failure or insufficient effort.
- Ask an SCR analyst to compare feasible layouts and durations using pilot
  estimates and simulations, including uncertainty in those estimates.

**Before scaling up:** agree what precision is useful for the management question.

\vspace{.5em}

\alert{A rough rule-of-thumb is that the full survey should generate \textbf{at least 10 recaptures and 10 individuals} (or else confidence intervals will be very wide)}

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 2--4 (pilot and feedback), 11--13, 20--23;
Durbach et al. (2021), https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13517.
No universal minimum number of individuals or spatial recaptures is taught. Precision
and bias depend jointly on density, detection, movement, effort and design.
A small pilot may give imprecise parameter estimates: explore a range of values. -->

## 3. Place each camera for identifiable images

\roomyitems[0.3em]

- Use randomization to decide on **broad areas** to locate arrays (i.e. 1x1km grid cell), but within each selected grid cell, choose the camera location **most likely to give a detection**.
- Use local knowledge and signs to choose routes or features used by the target species.
- Aim for clear views of identifying marks (e.g. flank patterns); test height,
  angle and distance, including likely travel directions.
- Adjust placement to body size, behaviour, camera model and terrain;
  inspect test images in the conditions expected during the survey.
- Use rapid image bursts, short trigger delays and suitable sensitivity;
  check night images and avoid glare or moving vegetation.

<!-- Source: PAWS (2020), pp. 25--27, generalised to the target species.
PAWS's 2--10 m camera-to-animal distance is a snow leopard example, not a
universal operating distance. Walk tests assess triggering/framing but must
also account for the target animal's height and likely speed.
PAWS suggests at least five rapid-fire photographs, high sensitivity and no
delay between encounters. Teach the purpose rather than impose settings on
all models: false triggers, battery use, snow and night blur must be tested.
Targeting trails within a representative array is distinct from selecting only
high-density landscapes. Record station microhabitat to model detection. -->

## 3. One camera or a pair at each station?

\roomyitems

- For species identified by flank patterns, paired cameras can photograph
  both sides during the same passage.
  Offset them to avoid facing flash directly into the other camera.
- Single cameras allow more stations with the same budget, if they provide
  enough views of the marks needed to identify that species.
- Test the trade-off in the pilot: how often can you assign a reliable ID?
- **A left-only and a right-only photograph cannot automatically be
  matched, or assumed to be different animals.**

Use one station ID for a paired setup, with separate equipment IDs.
Count each animal encounter once.

<!-- Source: PAWS (2020), pp. 25--26, 34--36.
Single-camera success in PAWS is conditional on image quality and behaviour;
do not transfer its high identification rates to every camera or site.
The teaching analysis assumes resolved individual identities. If identities
remain one-sided, agree a consistent usable side or seek specialist partial-
identity analysis; do not combine unmatched side catalogues as distinct animals.
Offset pairs and separate device/station IDs are practical implementation advice. -->

## 3. Log deployment, checks and failures

\roomyitems

- Assign permanent station and equipment IDs; record GPS coordinates,
  settings, habitat, installation time and a setup photograph.
- Synchronise clocks and record the time zone. At checks, note clock drift
  before resetting, and log card/battery changes.
- Plan safe maintenance and retrieval routes; carry spares appropriate
  for cold, snow and long access times.
- Record when each camera was working, obstructed, removed or moved.
  Give a relocated station a new location record.

\alert{No photograph at an operating station differs from no functioning camera.}
If the failure time is uncertain, record the uncertainty.

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 25--27, 33--34.
Clock/time-zone logs, failure uncertainty and equipment histories are practical
extensions of PAWS's installation/removal and effort requirements.
Do not infer uninterrupted operation merely because a camera was deployed.
Agree a documented rule for uncertain downtime with the analyst. Avoid moving
stations opportunistically during the main session without recording changes. -->

## 3. Genetic sampling: plan the search routes

\roomyitems

- Use mapped cells or watersheds to distribute **scat-search transects**
  across the landscape, including less promising habitat.
- Within them, follow safe routes where the species leaves scats (e.g.
  trails, riverbanks or marking sites); record omitted routes or sections.
- Repeat agreed routes in a short survey window; aim to find the same
  individuals at different locations.
- Save the **actual GPS track**, search date, distance/time, observers and
  conditions, including searches yielding no samples.

These are SCR search routes: no perpendicular-distance measurements are needed.

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 22--23, 29--30, 38--40;
Efford, M. (2011). Estimation of population density by spatially explicit
capture--recapture analysis of data from area searches. Ecology 92: 2202--2207.
https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0332.1
Efford, M. (2025). Polygon and transect detectors in secr 5.2.
https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-polygondetectors.pdf
PAWS gives 5 x 5 km cells as an example tied to movement scale, not a universal
grid specification. Routes can be targeted locally while representing habitat
across the landscape. They are not distance-sampling lines from Module 5. -->

## 3. Genetic sampling: link samples to effort

\roomyitems

- Agree collection, preservation, transport and quality checks with the
  laboratory **before** fieldwork; train everyone in the same protocol.
- Give each sample a unique ID linked to its exact GPS location, date,
  route/visit and field notes; prevent cross-contamination.
- Old scats may pre-date the survey. Agree how to handle sample age and
  prevent resampling the same deposit on later visits.
- Hair stations need mapped locations, regular checks and records of
  collection intervals and failures.
- Species and individual identity require laboratory confirmation.


<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 22--23, 29--30, 38--40;
Efford (2011), https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0332.1;
Efford (2025), https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-polygondetectors.pdf.
Do not prescribe storage chemistry in this introductory field lecture: arrange
it with the receiving lab. Collection date is not deposition date; aged scats
can violate closure. Discuss clearance/marking and revisit schedules locally.
Keep exact sample coordinates and searched routes even if later discretizing
into detector segments. Sample locations alone do not describe search effort.
Joint camera/genetic models are beyond this tutorial. -->

## 4. Individual IDs need a checked catalogue

\roomyitems

- Keep reference images for each individual, labelled by body side and marks.
  Compare several clear markings, rather than overall appearance.
- Have two trained reviewers assign IDs independently, then resolve
  disagreements and record the evidence for each decision.
- Retain uncertain images and mark them unresolved; seek expert review
  rather than inventing an ID. Record exclusions from the analysis.
- For genetic data, retain the laboratory's identity and quality decisions,
  including samples that failed.

\alert{Splitting one animal into several IDs will likely inflate abundance estimates.}

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 34--40;
Johansson, O., Samelius, G., Wikberg, E., Chapron, G., Mishra, C. & Low, M.
(2020). Identification errors in camera-trap studies result in systematic
population overestimation. Scientific Reports 10: 6393.
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-63367-z
PAWS recommends at least three comparable similarities/differences. Multiple
markings and independent checking reduce risk but cannot guarantee error-free
IDs. Never force uncertain matches based on proximity alone. Excluding many
poor images can also affect detection and inference: discuss with the analyst.
Keep a versioned catalogue and links back to the full image sequences. -->

## 4. Keep linked records, including zero effort

\small

| Record | Minimum information |
|:--|:--|
| Station | Station ID, coordinates, habitat, equipment IDs |
| Operation | Station ID, active intervals, checks, failures |
| Encounter | Station ID, date/time, individual ID, source images |
| Genetic search | Route/visit ID, GPS track, effort, sample IDs |

- Archive original images, GPS files and field sheets; keep backed-up copies
  separately from cleaned analysis tables.
- Use consistent IDs and a data dictionary. Check every encounter against
  the station location and operating dates.
- A burst of images is **one passage**, not one encounter per image.
  Agree encounter rules and analysis occasions with the analyst.

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 33--40;
Johansson et al. (2020), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-63367-z.
For the count-detector tutorial, repeated photographs within a visit must not
be counted as independent encounters. PAWS gives one hour as an example
separation rule; a universal time gap does not establish independence.
Retain raw timestamps to permit alternative event definitions and time effects.
Unresolved encounters should remain in the archive with an explicit status.
Restrict access to sensitive wildlife locations and photographs of people. -->

## 4. Prepare maps for the question and the model

\roomyitems

- Keep the reporting boundary, detector locations and search tracks
  as separate GIS layers.
- Use a suitable **projected coordinate system in metres**, with its CRS
  recorded; check GPS points on a map before analysis.
- For density questions, obtain a few justified covariate layers, such as
  terrain ruggedness, covering the whole modelled habitat region.
- Record local detection covariates at stations, such as camera type
  and trail/marking-site placement.
- The analyst needs habitat around the array as well as within it:
  animals with activity centres outside can still be detected inside.

<!-- Sources: PAWS (2020), pp. 33, 40, 44--47.
The reporting polygon, sampled area and model state-space/mask are distinct.
The state-space buffer must be checked for adequacy, as in the R tutorial;
do not clip it to an administrative boundary just because that is the reporting
region. Use matching CRS, units, extent/resolution and documented provenance
for covariates. Do not discard habitat solely for difficult access or no captures.
Complex mountain movement and unsampled habitat may require more advanced
models or a narrower scope of inference, with specialist advice. -->

## Before the main survey: review the four steps

\roomyitems

1. **Question and region:** a mapped target population and a realistic budget.
2. **Design and effort:** representative coverage, likely spatial recaptures,
   a suitable season and a pilot reviewed with an SCR analyst.
3. **Protocol:** trained teams, safe access, tested equipment and clear
   rules for checks, failures and any genetic collection.
4. **Data:** checked IDs, linked records, backups and GIS inputs.


<!-- Sources: synthesis of PAWS (2020), pp. 9--40, and the sources above.
Optional short discussion; 30 cameras is a hypothetical resource constraint,
not a recommended sample size. Possible responses: retrieval still needs
funding; pilot battery/storage performance; no opportunity to repair failures;
single versus paired stations; deployment timing, staffing, access and safety;
image processing and analysis costs. Ask whether the proposed design can meet
the stated goal, rather than selecting a spacing from the camera count alone. -->


# Analysis of SCR data with `secr`

## Spatial capture-recapture -- `secr`

`secr`, an `R` package for spatially explicit capture-recapture

- model fitting by maximum likelihood
    - efficient, nice properties
    - AIC-based model selection & model averaging
- Overview at
    - \url{https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/secr/vignettes/secr-overview.pdf}

\vspace{0.5cm}

```{r, eval=FALSE, size="scriptsize"}
install.packages("secr") 
library(secr)
?secr # overview vignette
```

## Demonstrating the `secr` workflow -- Pamir-Alai snow leopards {.t}

\roomyitems

Kyrgyzstan snow leopard example:

- Pamir-Alai mountains, Kyrgyzstan
- simulated camera-trap data (1 session)
- 35 detectors deployed (camera traps)
- one occasion covering the whole survey
- `r length(unique(preview_captures$id))` individuals detected, with `r nrow(preview_captures)` encounters

## Demonstrating the `secr` workflow -- Pamir-Alai snow leopards

Kyrgyzstan snow leopard example:

- Pamir-Alai mountains, Kyrgyzstan
- simulated camera-trap data (1 session)
- 35 detectors deployed (camera traps)
- one occasion covering the whole survey
- `r length(unique(preview_captures$id))` individuals detected, with `r nrow(preview_captures)` encounters

Read the two data files:

\vspace{0.2cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_cap_data <- read.csv("data/practical/snow_leopard_captures.csv")
sl_trap_data <- read.csv("data/practical/snow_leopard_traps.csv")
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
sl_cap_trapid <- sl_cap_data
sl_cap_xy <- merge(sl_cap_data, sl_trap_data)[, c("session", "id", "occasion", "x", "y")]
```

## SCR data structures - trap layout file {.t}

\roomyitems

Standard format for \alert{trap layout file} is a dataframe columns for:

- trap coordinates
    -  column names must be `x` and `y`
    - `secr` assumes all distances & coordinates are in meters
- trap identifier
    - can have any name

\vspace{0.25cm}

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[anchor=south east,xshift=-0.5cm,yshift=0.7cm] at (current page.south east){
\includegraphics[width=0.46\paperwidth]{figures/secr}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## SCR data structures - trap layout file

Standard format for \alert{trap layout file} is a dataframe columns for:

- trap coordinates (here `x`,`y`)
- trap identifier (here `trap`)
- trap usage (here `effort`)
- trap covariates (used to model **detectability**)

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines = 4}
sl_trap_data
```

\vspace{0.15cm}

- column order is important
- some column names are fixed (must be `x` and `y`), some are specified (`trap`), some are inferred from position (`effort`)
- `secr` assumes all distances & coordinates are in meters
 
## SCR data structures - convert to `traps` object

Need to convert the trap layout file to a `traps` object

- format the trap data using `?read.traps()`
    - identify coordinate and ID columns
    - define the detector type (`"count"` for these camera traps)
    - creates a `traps` class recognized by other functions (eg, `plot`, `summary`)

\vspace{0.25cm}
    
```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_traps <- read.traps(
  data = sl_trap_data[, c("trap", "x", "y", "effort")],
  trapID = "trap",
  detector = "count",
  binary.usage = FALSE)
```

```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines = 3}
sl_trap_data
```

## SCR data structures - camera effort

\roomyitems

- `effort` is the number of active camera-days during our single occasion.
- Most cameras operated for 90 days; six operated for 70--89 days.
- `binary.usage = FALSE` reads effort as numeric exposure.
- `secr` scales expected counts by effort: $\lambda_0$ is a rate per camera-day.

Inspect usage for any unusual values:

\vspace{0.2cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
table(usage(sl_traps))
```

```{r, eval=FALSE, size="scriptsize"}
plot(sl_traps)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, size="scriptsize", fig.align='center',fig.width=4,fig.height=3.5, out.width="92%", out.height="2.05in"}
plot(sl_traps, border = 3000, gridspace = 10000, detpar = list(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(0,0,0,0)))
```

The typical \alert{capture data} format is a data frame with columns for:

- a *session* identifier

- an individual identifier (*who*)
- capture occasion number (*when*)
- trap identifier (*where*)

## Associating captures and traps -- `make.capthist()`

\roomyitems

Create a `capthist` data object using `?make.capthist()`

- links sampling effort data and capture data 
- conducts a series of checks
- returns an analysis-ready data objects - `capthist`
- `make.capthist` requires the following:
    - the capture data
    - a `traps` object
    - the format of the capture data (we will use `"trapID"` exclusively)
    - the number of occasions

## Associating captures and traps -- `make.capthist()`

\roomyitems

Create a `capthist` data object using `?make.capthist()`

- links sampling effort data and capture data 
- conducts a series of checks
- returns an analysis-ready data objects - `capthist`
- `make.capthist` requires the following:

\vspace{0.25cm}
    
```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines = 5}
sl_ch <- make.capthist(captures = sl_cap_data, # capture file
                         traps = sl_traps,       # a traps object
                         fmt = "trapID",           # format of caps
                         noccasions = 1)           # number of occasions
```

## Two format options for capture data

Captures can be formatted using \alert{trap IDs} (`fmt = "trapID"`)

\vspace{0.1cm}
    
```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines = 4}
sl_cap_trapid
```

\vspace{0.5cm}

Captures can be formatted using \alert{coordinates directly} (`fmt = "XY"`)

\vspace{0.1cm}
    
```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines = 4}
sl_cap_xy
```

## Summarising the `capthist`

Extensive numerical summary of the SCR data:

```{r, size="compactcode"}
summary(sl_ch)
```

## Summarising the `capthist`

\roomyitems

Extensive numerical summary of the SCR data:

- `n`	inds detected on each occasion
- `u`	inds detected for the first time on each occasion
- `f`	number of inds detected on exactly `f` occasions
- `M(t+1)`	cumulative number of inds detected
- `losses`	inds not released on each occasion (mortality)
- `detections`	detections, including within-occasion `recaptures'
- `traps visited`	detectors with at least one detection
- `traps set`	number of detectors

## Defining the state-space {.t}

\roomyitems

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

- called a *mask* or *state-space*
    - defines where individuals can live
    - defines the population of interest
    - includes apparently un-sampled parts of the landscape

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[anchor=south east,xshift=-0.5cm,yshift=0.7cm] at (current page.south east){
\includegraphics[width=0.46\paperwidth]{figures/secr}};
\end{tikzpicture}



## Defining the state-space

\roomyitems

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

- called a *mask* or *state-space*
    - defines where individuals can live
    - defines the population of interest
    - includes apparently un-sampled parts of the landscape
- should include activity centres of all detectable individuals
    - use a buffer around traps
    - pr(detection) for individual with an AC outside area = 0
- for likelihood analysis, space is discrete
    - the mask is a fine mesh of points
    - integrate (*sum over*) the points

## Defining the state-space -- `make.mask()`

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

- the *mask* or *state-space* is a fine mesh of points defined by:
   - a buffer around traps
   - the spacing of the regular points
   - create using `?make.mask()`

\vspace{0.5cm}

## Defining the state-space -- `make.mask()`

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

- the *mask* or *state-space* is a fine mesh of points defined by:
   - a buffer around traps (conservatively `buffer = 30000`)
   - \textcolor{gray}{the spacing of the regular points}
   - \textcolor{gray}{create using \texttt{?make.mask()}}

```{r, size="scriptsize", warning=FALSE}
suggest.buffer(object = sl_ch, # a capthist object
               detectfn = "HHN")  # the detection function to be used
```

## Defining the state-space -- `make.mask()`

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

- the *mask* or *state-space* is a fine mesh of points defined by:
   - a buffer around traps (conservatively `buffer = 30000`)
   - the spacing of the regular points (conservatively `spacing = 1500`)
   - \textcolor{gray}{create using \texttt{?make.mask()}}

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mask <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps, # a traps object
                       buffer = 30000,      # the buffer
                       spacing = 1500)     # mask spacing
```

 


## Defining the state-space -- `make.mask()`

Area sampled extends beyond detector array -- this area is part of the SCR model!

\vspace{0.15cm}

```{r, eval=FALSE, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mask <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps, buffer = 30000, spacing = 1500)
plot(sl_mask)                      # plot the mask
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
plot(sl_ch, tracks=TRUE, add=TRUE) # add the captures
```

\vspace{0.1cm}

```{r, echo=FALSE, size="scriptsize", fig.align='center',fig.width=6,fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, message = FALSE, out.width="92%", out.height="1.6in"}
sl_mask <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps, buffer = 30000, spacing = 1500)
plot(sl_mask, cex = 0.5)                      # plot the mask
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
plot(sl_ch, tracks=TRUE, rad = 600, add=TRUE, cappar = list(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(0,0,0,0)))
```

## Defining the state-space -- `make.mask()`

A more efficient mask only keeps points within distance `buffer` (in m) of any trap.

\vspace{0.15cm}

```{r, eval=FALSE, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mask <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps, buffer = 30000,
                     spacing = 1500, type = "trapbuffer")
plot(sl_mask)                      # plot the mask
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
plot(sl_ch, tracks=TRUE, add=TRUE) # add the captures
```

\vspace{0.1cm}

```{r, echo=FALSE, size="scriptsize", fig.align='center',fig.width=6,fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, message = FALSE, out.width="92%", out.height="1.6in"}
sl_mask <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps, buffer = 30000,
                     spacing = 1500, type = "trapbuffer")
plot(sl_mask, cex = 0.5)                      # plot the mask
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
plot(sl_ch, tracks=TRUE, rad = 600, add=TRUE, cappar = list(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(0,0,0,0)))
```

## Defining the state-space -- two masks

- **Model fitting mask** (`sl_mask`): the area integrated over when fitting
  the model with `secr.fit()`.
- **Prediction mask** (`pamir_alai_region`): the area over which we predict
  density or calculate abundance with `region.N()`.

Create a prediction mask for the full Pamir-Alai survey region:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
survey_area <- sf::st_read(
  "data/survey_area/pamir_alai_kyrgyzstan_utm43.gpkg",
  quiet = TRUE)
pamir_alai_region <- make.mask(traps = sl_traps,
                               type = "polygon",
                               poly = survey_area,
                               spacing = 1500)
```

Need to add any spatial covariates you want to predict with

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
# read in e.g. ruggedness raster
tri_raster <- terra::rast("data/spatial_covs/tri_KYRG.tif")
# add to mask
pamir_alai_region <- addCovariates(pamir_alai_region, tri_raster)
```

## Defining the state-space -- two masks

Plotting the prediction and model-fitting masks, with trap locations. 

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, out.width="92%", out.height="2.65in"}
plot(pamir_alai_region, dots = FALSE, col = "grey85", polycol = "grey40")
plot(sl_mask, dots = FALSE, col = "lightsteelblue", add = TRUE)
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
legend("bottom", legend = c("Prediction mask", "Model fitting mask", "Camera traps"),
       pch = c(15, 15, 3), col = c("grey85", "lightsteelblue", "red"),
       horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```

## Model fitting using `secr.fit`

To fit models in `secr`:

- use the fitting function `secr.fit()`
- provide the following three objects required to fit a model: 
    - the `capthist` object (`capthist=`)
    - a list specifying the model (`model =`)
    - the `mask` object (`mask=`)

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize", eval=FALSE}
mod <- secr.fit(capthist=, # capthist object
                model=,    # model specification
                mask=)     # the mask
```

## Specifying the SCR model in `secr.fit`

The `model` components define linear predictor for each model component

- a list with 3 formulae: `list(D~, lambda0~, sigma~)`
    - `D~`: model describing variation in density
    - `lambda0~`: model describing variation in baseline encounter rate
    - `sigma~`: model describing variation in sigma

- baseline density, baseline detection model given by `model = list(D~1, lambda0~1, sigma~1)`. This sets
$$\text{log}(D(s_i)) = \beta_0 \quad
\text{log}(\lambda_0) = \alpha_0 \quad
\text{log}(\sigma) = \gamma_0$$

- logs are there to make sure density and detection rates are positive.

## Fitting the null model -- SCR~0~

Let's fit the null SCR model to the Pamir-Alai data

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r, size = "scriptsize", output.lines=14, warning=FALSE, message = FALSE}
sl_mod <- secr.fit(capthist = sl_ch,
                     model = list(D~1, lambda0~1, sigma~1), 
                     mask = sl_mask,
                     detectfn = "HHN",
                     trace = FALSE)
```

## Fitting the null model -- SCR~0~

Type the name of the model for a model summary:

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r,eval=TRUE, size="scriptsize", output.lines=15}
sl_mod # 1 of 3
```

Type the name of the model for a model summary:

\vspace{0.05cm}

```{r,eval=TRUE, size="scriptsize", output.lines=16:31}
sl_mod # 2 of 3
```

## Modelling density -- terrain ruggedness

Define the model for \alert{density}

$$\text{log}(D(s_i)) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{tri}(s_i)$$

- density varies with terrain ruggedness (TRI)
- TRI is supplied for each mask point from the local terrain raster
- formula syntax: `D~tri`

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mask <- addCovariates(sl_mask, tri_raster, columns = "tri")
mask_data <- covariates(sl_mask)
```

## Terrain ruggedness across the mask

TRI at each mask point, with camera locations overlaid:

```{r, size="scriptsize", fig.align="center", fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5, out.width="92%", out.height="2.05in"}
covariates(sl_mask)$TRI <- covariates(sl_mask)$tri
plot(sl_mask, covariate = "TRI", dots = FALSE, breaks = 6)
plot(sl_traps, add = TRUE)
```

## Fitting a density covariate -- SCR~tri~

Let's fit a model with density varying with terrain ruggedness

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize", output.lines=14}
sl_mod_tri <- secr.fit(capthist = sl_ch,
                      model = list(D~tri, lambda0~1, sigma~1),
                      mask = sl_mask,
                      detectfn = "HHN",
                      start = sl_mod,
                      method = "Nelder-Mead",
                      trace = FALSE)
```

## Comparing models -- `AIC()`

Compare constant density with density varying with terrain ruggedness

\vspace{0.25cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
AIC(sl_mod, sl_mod_tri)
```

- smaller AIC indicates the better-supported model
- the terrain model estimates one extra parameter

## Modelling detection -- camera type

Define the model for \alert{baseline encounter rate}

$$\text{log}(\lambda_0) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_B\,\text{camera type}$$

- compare camera types `A` and `B` (`A` is the reference)
- keep `D~tri` and `sigma~1`

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mod_camera <- secr.fit(capthist = sl_ch,
                         model = list(D~tri, lambda0~camera_type, sigma~1),
                         mask = sl_mask,
                         detectfn = "HHN",
                         start = sl_mod_tri,
                         method = "Nelder-Mead",
                         trace = FALSE)
```

## Modelling detection -- distance to water

$$\text{log}(\lambda_0) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\,\text{d2water}$$

Distance to water is expressed in kilometres:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
sl_mod_water <- secr.fit(capthist = sl_ch,
                        model = list(D~tri, lambda0~d2water, sigma~1),
                        mask = sl_mask,
                        detectfn = "HHN",
                        start = sl_mod_tri,
                        method = "Nelder-Mead",
                        trace = FALSE)
```

## Comparing detection models -- `AIC()`

Compare the density and detection models:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
AIC(sl_mod, sl_mod_tri, sl_mod_camera, sl_mod_water)
```

- the detection models keep `D~tri` and `sigma~1`
- does adding camera type or distance to water improve support?

## Post processing functions in `secr`

\roomyitems

A bunch of helper functions for working with model output:

- extract link-scale estimates & associated uncertainty: `?coef()`
- extract real-scale estimates & associated uncertainty: `?predict()`
- compute the population size for the area: `region.N()`
- plot detection function based on estimates: `plot()`
- plot probability contours for estimated $\mathbf{s}_i$: `fxi.contour()`
- $\ldots$ more post-processing functions (`?secr`)

## Extract parameter estimates -- \newline `coef()`, `predict()` & `region.N()`

Link-scale estimates & uncertainty: `coef()`

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
coef(sl_mod)
```

\vspace{0.4cm}

Response-scale estimates & uncertainty: `predict()`

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
predict(sl_mod)
```


## Best model -- `coef()`

Link-scale estimates for `D~tri`, `lambda0~camera_type`, `sigma~1`:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
coef(sl_mod_camera)
```

- `D.tri`: change in log-density per unit of terrain ruggedness
- `lambda0.camera_typeB`: change in log-encounter rate for B relative to A

Camera B's baseline encounter rate is `r round(exp(coef(sl_mod_camera)["lambda0.camera_typeB", "beta"]), 1)` times that of camera A.

## Best model -- `predict()`

Response-scale estimates across terrain ruggedness and camera types:

\vspace{0.2cm}

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
prediction_data <- expand.grid(tri = c(15, 35, 55),
                               camera_type = c("A", "B"))
predict(sl_mod_camera, newdata = prediction_data, se.fit = FALSE)
```

- density changes with terrain ruggedness
- camera type changes the baseline encounter rate (per camera-day)
- the spatial scale $\sigma$ is shared by both camera types

## Extract abundance estimates -- `region.N()`

\small
\setbeamerfont{itemize/enumerate body}{size=\small}

Abundance within the fitting mask:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
region.N(sl_mod_tri)
```

Extrapolate to the full Pamir-Alai survey region:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
pamir_alai_region <- readRDS("data/practical/pamir_alai_region.rds")
region.N(sl_mod_tri, region = pamir_alai_region)
```

- `E.N` is **expected abundance**: the expected number of animals under the fitted density model.
- `R.N` is **realised abundance**: the estimated number actually present during this survey.
- `E.N` uses the expected number of *detected* animals, `R.N` uses the actual number detected.

## Density and terrain ruggedness -- `predict()`

Response-scale density estimates at different terrain ruggedness values:

```{r, size="scriptsize"}
predict(sl_mod_tri, newdata = data.frame(tri = c(15, 35, 55)))
```

## Density and terrain ruggedness

How does estimated density change with terrain ruggedness?

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, out.width="92%", out.height="2.05in"}
tri_values <- seq(quantile(mask_data$tri, 0.05),
                  quantile(mask_data$tri, 0.95), length.out = 100)
tri_predictions <- predict(sl_mod_tri, newdata = data.frame(tri = tri_values))
density_est <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tri_predictions, function(x) x["D", ]))
plot(tri_values, density_est$estimate * 10000, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Terrain ruggedness (TRI)",
     ylab = expression("Snow leopards per 100 " * km^2),
     ylim = c(0, max(density_est$ucl * 10000)))
polygon(c(tri_values, rev(tri_values)),
        c(density_est$lcl, rev(density_est$ucl)) * 10000,
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.2), border = NA)
lines(tri_values, density_est$estimate * 10000, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue4")
```

## Plot detection function -- `plot()`

The fitted hazard half-normal detection function:

```{r, size="scriptsize", fig.align='center',fig.width=6,fig.height=5, warning=FALSE, out.width="92%", out.height="1.85in"}
plot(x = sl_mod,                 # the fitted model
     limits = TRUE,                # plot CIs
     xval = seq(0,30000,length=60)) # limits of the x (distance) axis 
```


## Detection functions -- camera types A and B

Compare the two camera types using the best model:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
```

```{r, size="scriptsize", fig.align="center", fig.width=6, fig.height=4, out.width="92%", out.height="1.5in"}
camera_types <- data.frame(tri = 35,
                           camera_type = factor(c("A", "B")))
distances <- seq(0, 30000, by = 500)
plot(sl_mod_camera, newdata = camera_types[2, ], col = "red", xval = distances)
plot(sl_mod_camera, newdata = camera_types[1, ], col = "blue",
     xval = distances, add = TRUE)
legend("topright", c("Camera A", "Camera B"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

## What to report

A useful report states:

- Species, eligible animals, survey region and dates.

- Detector layout, actual effort, identification method, number of
  individuals detected and spatial recaptures.

- Detector type, detection function and models for density and detection;
  model comparisons and checks of convergence and mask/buffer sensitivity.

- Density with units, abundance for a clearly mapped region, and
  confidence intervals. State whether abundance is expected or realised.

- Assumptions, identification uncertainty and limits to extrapolation.

Keep reporting region distinct from the fitting mask; density units must be
explicit, especially when converting secr's default per-hectare output.
Report checks actually performed and unresolved limitations. The classroom
dataset is simulated: its estimates are not population estimates for Kyrgyzstan. -->
